subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What did the initials HUAC stand for?
options: House Un-American Activities Committee
Highly Urgent Anti-Communist Agency
House Union of American Citizens
Homeland Un-American Alliance Council
questions.explain: HUAC was the congressional committee that investigated alleged communist activity, including in Hollywood.

questions.q: In February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed to hold a list of communists working in the State Department during a speech in which town?
options: Wheeling, West Virginia
Topeka, Kansas
Little Rock, Arkansas
Montgomery, Alabama
questions.explain: McCarthy's Wheeling speech launched his high-profile anti-communist campaign.

questions.q: Why did the Soviet Union's first successful atomic bomb test in 1949 intensify the Red Scare in the USA?
options: It made Americans fear that spies had passed nuclear secrets to the USSR
It proved that McCarthy's list of names was accurate
It caused the USA to lose the Korean War
It led directly to the building of the Berlin Wall
questions.explain: The USSR's rapid development of the bomb fuelled fears of communist infiltration and espionage.

questions.q: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953 after being convicted of what?
options: Passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union
Leading a communist uprising in Hollywood
Organising the Montgomery Bus Boycott
Refusing to testify before the Senate
questions.explain: The Rosenbergs were convicted of espionage for passing nuclear secrets to the USSR.

questions.q: The group of film industry figures blacklisted in 1947 for refusing to answer HUAC's questions became known as?
options: The Hollywood Ten
The Little Rock Nine
The Freedom Riders
The Greensboro Four
questions.explain: The Hollywood Ten were jailed and blacklisted for refusing to cooperate with HUAC.

questions.q: What brought about the decline of Joseph McCarthy's influence in 1954?
options: Televised hearings exposed his bullying tactics and the Senate censured him
He was imprisoned for treason
He was defeated in a presidential election
The Supreme Court banned HUAC
questions.explain: The televised Army-McCarthy hearings damaged his reputation and the Senate formally censured him in 1954.

questions.q: In 1951 a civil servant is dismissed from a government post merely because of a rumour that he once attended a communist meeting, with no evidence presented. This treatment best reflects which feature of the period?
options: The climate of suspicion created by the Red Scare and loyalty checks
The impact of the Civil Rights Act
The success of the Freedom Rides
The aims of the Black Panther Party
questions.explain: Loyalty checks meant people could lose jobs on mere suspicion, reflecting Red Scare paranoia.

questions.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court ruling declared segregation in state schools unconstitutional?
options: Brown v Board of Education of Topeka
Plessy v Ferguson
Roe v Wade
Browder v Gayle
questions.explain: Brown v Board overturned the idea that segregated schools could be 'separate but equal'.

questions.q: Whose arrest in Montgomery in December 1955 triggered the bus boycott?
options: Rosa Parks
Ella Baker
Coretta Scott King
Daisy Bates
questions.explain: Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat, sparking the boycott.

questions.q: What was the main outcome of the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56)?
options: The Supreme Court ruled that segregation on buses was unconstitutional
The Civil Rights Act was immediately passed
African Americans gained the right to vote
Schools across the South were desegregated
questions.explain: The year-long boycott ended when the Supreme Court declared bus segregation unconstitutional.

questions.q: Why was the Little Rock crisis of 1957 significant?
options: It showed the federal government was prepared to use troops to enforce desegregation
It ended segregation on all public transport
It marked the founding of the NAACP
It gave women the right to vote
questions.explain: President Eisenhower sent federal troops to protect the black students and enforce integration.

questions.q: The 1896 Supreme Court case that established the 'separate but equal' doctrine was?
options: Plessy v Ferguson
Brown v Board of Education
Dred Scott v Sandford
Browder v Gayle
questions.explain: Plessy v Ferguson legalised segregation under the 'separate but equal' principle.

questions.q: Why was television coverage of the Birmingham campaign in 1963 important for the civil rights movement?
options: Images of police using dogs and fire hoses on peaceful protesters won public sympathy
It showed McCarthy questioning witnesses
It broadcast Malcolm X's conversion to non-violence
It proved the boycott of buses had failed
questions.explain: Televised brutality against peaceful protesters shocked the nation and built support for reform.

questions.q: At the 1963 March on Washington, Martin Luther King delivered which famous speech?
options: "I Have a Dream"
"The Ballot or the Bullet"
"We Shall Overcome"
"Ask Not What Your Country Can Do"
questions.explain: King's 'I Have a Dream' speech became a defining moment of the civil rights movement.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
options: It made discrimination and segregation in public places and employment illegal
It gave the vote to eighteen-year-olds
It ended the Vietnam War
It banned the Ku Klux Klan
questions.explain: The 1964 Act outlawed segregation and discrimination in public facilities and jobs.

questions.q: In 1960 a group of black students sit at a whites-only lunch counter and refuse to leave when denied service. Which method of protest are they using?
options: Non-violent direct action (a sit-in)
Armed self-defence
A legal challenge in the Supreme Court
A general labour strike
questions.explain: The Greensboro-style sit-ins were a form of peaceful, non-violent direct action.

questions.q: Why did some younger activists turn towards 'Black Power' in the mid-1960s?
options: They were frustrated by the slow pace of change and wanted black pride and self-reliance
They wanted to strengthen ties with the Ku Klux Klan
They rejected the idea of black equality
They supported the aims of Senator McCarthy
questions.explain: Black Power reflected impatience with gradual reform and a desire for black pride and self-determination.

questions.q: The Black Panther Party ran free breakfast programmes and health clinics in poor black neighbourhoods. What does this best show about the party?
options: It combined militancy with community self-help programmes
It rejected all forms of community organisation
It supported segregation
It worked closely with HUAC
questions.explain: Alongside its militant image, the Panthers ran social programmes to support black communities.

questions.q: How did Malcolm X's early views differ from those of Martin Luther King?
options: He rejected non-violence and integration, favouring black separatism and self-defence
He believed only in legal challenges through the courts
He argued that African Americans should not vote
He supported the 'separate but equal' doctrine
questions.explain: Early on, Malcolm X advocated black separatism and self-defence rather than King's non-violent integration.

questions.q: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, two African American athletes raised black-gloved fists on the podium. This gesture was intended to?
options: Protest against racism and show support for Black Power
Celebrate the passing of the Civil Rights Act
Support the Vietnam War
Oppose the Montgomery Bus Boycott
questions.explain: Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists as a Black Power salute against racial injustice.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE History (4HI1) specification; A Divided Union: USA 1945-70
